# The Useful Lies of Maps

In 1946, Jorge Luis Borges wrote a story that fits in a single paragraph. It describes an empire so devoted to cartography that its mapmakers eventually produce a map of the empire at the scale of the empire itself — a map that coincides with the territory point for point. Succeeding generations, being less fond of the art, recognize the thing as useless and abandon it to the weather. In the western deserts, tattered ruins of the map remain, sheltering animals and beggars.

The joke has a sharp edge: a perfect map is a failure. Cartography's first commandment is *thou shalt shrink*, and from that commandment everything else follows. A map is useful precisely insofar as it betrays the world — omitting, simplifying, flattening, exaggerating. The philosopher Alfred Korzybski coined the famous warning that "the map is not the territory," but the corollary gets less attention: a map that *were* the territory would be no map at all. Every map ever drawn is a set of decisions about which truths matter and which can be sacrificed. The history of cartography, then, is really a history of what civilizations cared about. And what they got wrong. Especially what they got wrong.

## The Peel Problem

Take an orange and peel it in one piece. Now try to press the peel flat against a table. It tears. It always tears. In 1827, Carl Friedrich Gauss proved this wasn't a failure of technique but a law of the universe: his *Theorema Egregium* — "remarkable theorem," and Gauss was not a man given to hype — shows that curvature is intrinsic to a surface. A sphere curves one way, a plane another, and no amount of cleverness moves between them without stretching or ripping something. Every flat map of the round Earth is a scar, a record of where the mapmaker decided the tearing would happen.

Consider the most famous scar of all: the Mercator projection, 1569. It is routinely denounced today as a distortion machine, which it is, but the denunciations often skip the part where it was a work of genius built for a specific job. Draw a straight line between two ports on a Mercator map and that line gives you a constant compass bearing — a course a sailor can actually hold. For the age of sail, that was worth almost any price.

The price was steep, though. Because longitude lines stay parallel instead of converging at the poles, scale inflates as you move toward the top and bottom of the map. Greenland, about 2.2 million square kilometers, swells until it looks the size of Africa — which is actually fourteen times larger. Alaska appears to rival Brazil; Brazil is five times bigger. Entire generations of schoolchildren absorbed a planet where the wealthy northern latitudes loom enormous and the equatorial world, where most humans actually live, politely shrinks.

In 1973, a German historian named Arno Peters called a press conference to unveil what he presented as a revolutionary corrective: an equal-area projection that gave every region its honest share of the page. Cartographers pointed out, with some heat, that James Gall had published the identical mathematics in 1855, and that equal-area maps of various flavors had existed for ages. The ensuing fight was wonderfully bitter, and it was never really about math. It was about whose distortion gets to call itself neutral. That's the deep lesson: a projection is an ideology you can compute. The question is never whether a map is accurate. The question is accurate *for what*, and *for whom*.

## Sermons on Vellum

If you want to see a map that makes no pretense of neutrality, go to Hereford Cathedral, where the largest surviving medieval world map hangs — drawn around 1300 on a single calfskin more than five feet across. East sits at the top, which is where our word "orientation" comes from: *oriens*, the rising sun. Jerusalem stands at the center. Christ in Majesty presides above the rim of the world, Eden glows near the top, and the British Isles huddle at the lower-left edge, about as far from salvation as geography permits. Around the margins wander the marvels: dog-headed men, and the sciapods, the one-legged people said to recline in the shade of their own enormous foot.

You could not navigate to the pub with the Hereford map. That was never its job. It is a sermon in vellum — a map not of where things are but of what things mean. The geography is theology wearing a costume.

Around the same centuries, Mediterranean sailors were using something with the opposite soul: the portolan chart. These were pure instruments — coastlines rendered with startling accuracy, interiors left empty, the whole sheet webbed with "rhumb lines" radiating from compass roses in red, green, and brown ink. Nothing sacred anywhere on them. Just: here is the coast, here are your bearings, try not to die. Two cartographic traditions, one species — the map as worldview and the map as wrench.

The Pacific offered a third answer that humbles both. Marshall Islands navigators built "stick charts" from palm ribs lashed together, cowrie shells marking islands, curved sticks encoding the patterns of ocean swells and how those swells bend and reflect around land. Here's the astonishing part: the charts were teaching tools, memorized on shore. Navigators didn't carry them to sea — they carried the knowledge *in their bodies*, feeling the swell patterns through the hull in the dark. It was a map of motion rather than objects, the ocean read like sheet music. Western cartography spent millennia mapping the world's surfaces. These sailors mapped its rhythms.

As for the monsters: "here be dragons" is the most famous phrase in cartography, and it almost never appeared. The Latin *hic sunt dracones* survives in earnest on essentially one early object, a copper globe from around 1510 now in the New York Public Library, off the coast of Asia. Most mapmakers faced the unknown with blank parchment instead, which requires a different kind of nerve. A monster is at least a claim. A blank is an admission — and an invitation.

## Islands That Never Were

Blanks are one failure mode. Invention is another, and the invented places are where cartography gets truly strange.

West of Ireland, on charts dating back to 1325, sits an island called Hy-Brasil — circular, often split by a river, drawn with complete confidence by mapmaker after mapmaker. Irish legend said it surfaced from the mist once every seven years. Sailors reported sightings; expeditions went looking. It clung to respectable charts well into the nineteenth century: five hundred years of a place that never existed.

Frisland was worse, because Frisland was born of a hoax. In 1558, a Venetian named Nicolò Zeno published an account claiming his ancestors had roamed the North Atlantic in the 1390s, complete with a map showing a large island south of Iceland. The voyage is now considered a fabrication top to bottom, but no matter — Frisland wandered through serious maps for more than a century, drifting around the ocean like a rumor that refused to die.

Then there's California. The name itself comes from a 1510 Spanish romance novel — an island of gold and griffins ruled by the warrior queen Calafia. When Spanish explorers reached the long peninsula on the Pacific coast, they named it after this fictional island and then, with perfect poetic consistency, spent the better part of two centuries drawing it *as* an island. Even after Father Eusebio Kino's overland journeys around 1700 proved California was firmly attached to the continent, the island lingered on European charts. Spain finally issued a royal decree in 1747 clarifying that California was not, in fact, an island — which ranks among the more delightful sentences any government has ever been forced to publish.

Why did these errors outlive the evidence against them? Because mapmakers copied mapmakers. A line already printed carried an authority that no sailor's testimony could match. The map didn't merely fail to describe the territory; on occasion, it bullied the territory for centuries.

## The Woman Who Drew the Bottom of the Ocean

The twentieth century flipped the whole problem over. By then the coasts were known, the interiors filled in. The great blank had moved underwater.

Marie Tharp arrived at Columbia's Lamont Observatory in 1948, hired as a draftsperson. Women weren't permitted on the research vessels — it was considered bad luck to have one aboard — so while ships crossed the oceans towing echo sounders, Tharp stayed on land, converting thousands of depth soundings into hand-drawn profiles of a seafloor no human had ever seen.

In 1952, plotting the North Atlantic, she noticed something odd in the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge: a deep V-shaped notch, a rift valley running right down the ridge's spine. A valley like that implied the seafloor was splitting apart — which implied the continents drifted, then considered a crank theory on par with Atlantis. She showed it to her colleague Bruce Heezen. His response, as she later told it, was to dismiss it as "girl talk."

But Heezen happened to be mapping earthquake epicenters, and the earthquakes kept landing along the exact same line as Tharp's rift. The alignment was too precise to wave away. Within years, the evidence snowballed into plate tectonics — the unifying theory of the Earth sciences, as revolutionary for geology as evolution was for biology. The mid-ocean ridge turned out to be a single mountain range some 40,000 miles long, the largest geological feature on the planet, and the rift was its open seam: the place where the Earth continuously manufactures new crust. Our planet has a wound that never closes, and the wound is where the world is born.

Tharp kept drawing. Her maps, transformed into luminous painted panoramas in collaboration with the artist Heinrich Berann, reached millions through *National Geographic* in 1977 and still shape what most of us picture when we picture the ocean floor. Her verdict on the long fight over credit: "I was so busy making maps I let them argue." And late in life, looking back: "Not too many people can say this about their lives: the whole world was spread out before me."

Here's the twist her story leaves us with. We have now mapped essentially all of the Moon and Mars in high resolution — while only about a quarter of our own seafloor has been surveyed with modern sonar. Satellites can't help; radar and light stop at the water's surface. The greatest terra incognita remaining to us isn't on some other world. It's downstairs, under two miles of cold dark water, right here. The blank never went away. It sank.

## The Extinction of Lost

Which brings us to the blue dot.

Somewhere above you, a couple of dozen satellites whisper precise timing signals; your phone compares them, triangulates, and a serene little circle announces *you are here*. It is the most democratic cartographic achievement in human history — billions of people walking around with a map finer than anything a Renaissance emperor could have purchased at any price. And something quiet went extinct in the process.

Being lost used to be an ordinary human experience: the wrong exit, the paper map unfolded across the steering wheel, the debate about whether to stop and ask someone. It had a texture — mild panic, then curiosity, occasionally grace. London cab drivers who spend years memorizing the city's 25,000 streets for "the Knowledge" develop measurably larger posterior hippocampi, the brain region tied to spatial memory; some research suggests that perpetual reliance on turn-by-turn directions lets that machinery idle and weaken. Park rangers in the American West coined the grim phrase "death by GPS" for travelers who follow the blue line onto closed desert roads and keep going, trusting the map over their own eyes — the phantom-island problem, shrunk to dashboard size.

The urban theorist Kevin Lynch argued that each of us carries a mental map of our city built from five elements — paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks — and that this inner atlas is how a place becomes *ours*. The blue dot quietly outsources the whole construction. And notice the catch in the word "lost" itself: you can only be lost if you hold some belief about where you ought to be. The dot doesn't answer the question. It dissolves it, which is a strange new way of never quite being anywhere at all.

## The Honest Scar

So: all maps lie. They have to; the orange peel tears. But lies differ in their honesty, and the best maps are the ones that confess — that wear their distortions openly if you know how to read them, the way Mercator's grid admits its crime in the spacing of its lines.

And maybe that's the final thing maps teach us. Not where things are, but that the world is worth the trouble of describing — knowable enough to attempt, strange enough to keep attempting forever. A map can even be an argument that changes the world: when John Snow plotted cholera deaths across London in 1854, the dots clustered around a single water pump on Broad Street, and the case made itself. Every map, right or wrong, is a wager that the territory rewards the trip. The dragons were never the point. The going was.

Gauss proved in 1827 that no amount of cleverness avoids this: his Theorema Egregium ("remarkable theorem" — Gauss wasn't modest) shows curvature is intrinsic to a surface; you can't move from sphere to plane without stretching or tearing something. Tharp kept drawing. Her maps, painted into gorgeous physiographic panoramas with the artist Heinrich Berann, reached the public through National Geographic in 1977 and still define what most of us picture when we picture the seafloor. Her summary of the credit wars: "I was so busy making maps I let them argue." Later in life: "Not too many people can say this about their lives: The whole world was spread out before me."

Now consider the blue dot. A couple dozen satellites whisper timing signals; your phone triangulates; a serene circle announces: you are here. It is the most democratic cartographic achievement in history — billions of people carry a map better than anything a 16th-century emperor could buy.

# The Useful Lies of Maps

Opening: In the middle of the twentieth century... no wait, Borges wrote 1946. "In 1946, Jorge Luis Borges wrote a one-paragraph short story about an empire..." Good. Actually the story: "Del rigor en la ciencia" — "On Exactitude in Science." The map coincides point for point with the empire; succeeding generations find it cumbersome and abandon it to the elements; in the western deserts, tattered ruins shelter animals and beggars.

Then: the lesson cuts both ways. A map the size of the territory is useless. Cartography's first commandment: thou shalt shrink. Every map is a betrayal of the world, and the betrayal is the point.

Korzybski: "A map is not the territory" — 1931. But add the lesser-known corollary: a map that were the territory would be no map at all.

Thesis: every map is a set of choices about what to omit, exaggerate, flatten, invent. The history of cartography is a history of which truths a civilization cared about.

Section 2: Why the world won't hold still for paper.

Take an orange. Peel it. Try to press the peel flat — it tears. Gauss proved in 1827 that no amount of cleverness avoids this: his Theorema Egregium ("remarkable theorem" — Gauss wasn't modest) shows curvature is intrinsic to a surface; you can't move from sphere to plane without stretching or tearing something. Every flat map of the round Earth is a record of where the mapmaker decided the tearing would happen.

Mercator, 1569. What it's actually for: draw a line between two ports on a Mercator map and it gives you a constant compass bearing. For a sailor, that's gold. The cost: scale grows toward the poles; the grid stays rectangular; shapes near the poles inflate. Greenland (~2.2M km²) looks Africa-sized; Africa (~30M km²) is fourteen times larger. Brazil is five times the size of Alaska, and you'd never know it. Whole generations absorbed a world where the rich northern temperate zones loom and the equatorial world shrinks.

1973, Arno Peters, press conference: presented the Peters projection (identical math to James Gall's 1855 version) as a corrective, equal-area. The cartographic establishment was furious — partly at the grandstanding, partly at the claim of novelty. UNESCO etc. adopted it. The fight wasn't about math; it was about whose distortion counts as neutral. Lesson: a projection is an ideology you can compute. The question is never whether a map is accurate but accurate for what.

Section 3: The map as a worldview.

Hereford, c. 1300. Single calfskin. East on top — that's where "orientation" comes from (oriens, the rising sun). Jerusalem at the center; Christ in Majesty above; Eden near the top; the British Isles tucked at the lower left edge, about as far from salvation as geography allows. Around the margins: marvels — dog-headed men, the sciapods who recline in their own foot's shade. You couldn't navigate to the pub with it. That wasn't its job. It was a sermon in vellum: a map of what mattered, not where things are.

Portolan charts, 13th century Mediterranean: the opposite soul. Coastlines startlingly accurate; interiors empty; webs of rhumb lines in red, green, brown ink radiating from compass roses. Nothing theological. Just: here is the coast, here are the bearings, don't die.

And a third answer from the Pacific: Marshall Islands stick charts — palm ribs lashed together, cowrie shells for islands, curved sticks for ocean swells and how they refract around land. Navigators memorized them ashore; they weren't carried on voyages. A map of motion, of patterns in water — the sea read like sheet music. Western cartography mapped the world's surfaces; these mapped its rhythms.

"Hic sunt dracones" — almost never actually written. The famous phrase appears in earnest on essentially one surviving object, the Hunt-Lenox globe (~1510), off the coast of Asia. Mostly mapmakers left the unknown blank, which takes a different kind of nerve than filling it with monsters. A monster is at least a claim. A blank is an invitation.

Section 4: The islands that weren't there.

If blanks are one failure mode, invention is another. Hy-Brasil: a phantom island west of Ireland, from Irish legend; appears on portolan charts from 1325 (the Dalorto chart); circular, bisected by a river; said to surface from the mist once every seven years. Expeditions claimed sightings. It clung to reputable charts into the 19th century — five hundred years of a place that never was.

Frisland: born from a hoax. In 1558 a Venetian published an account of his ancestors, the Zeno brothers, supposedly exploring the North Atlantic in the 1390s; the accompanying map invented Frisland, a large island south of Iceland. The voyage was almost certainly fabricated, but Frisland kept appearing on serious maps for more than a century, migrating around the ocean like a rumor.

California: the name comes from a 1510 Spanish romance, an island of gold and griffins ruled by Queen Calafia. When Spanish explorers reached the peninsula, they named it after a fictional island and then — fittingly — mapped it as one. For over a century much of Europe drew California adrift. Father Eusebio Kino's overland journeys around 1700 proved it was attached to the continent, and still the island lingered; Spain issued a royal decree in 1747 clarifying that California was not, in fact, an island, which is among the more delightful sentences any government has had to issue.

Why did these errors outlive the evidence? Because mapmakers copied mapmakers. A line already printed had authority that a sailor's testimony lacked. The map didn't just fail to describe the territory — it bullied it.

Section 5: The woman who mapped the bottom of the world.

The twentieth century flipped the script: the coasts were known; the blank moved underwater. Marie Tharp, hired at Columbia's Lamont Observatory in 1948 as a draftsperson. Women weren't allowed on the research vessels — bad luck, it was said — so while ships crossed the Atlantic dragging echo sounders, Tharp stayed ashore turning their soundings into profiles of the seafloor.

In 1952, plotting the North Atlantic, she noticed something in the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge: a deep V-shaped notch, a rift valley running down the ridge's spine. A valley like that implied the seafloor was being pulled apart — which implied continental drift, then considered a crank theory. She showed it to her colleague Bruce Heezen. His response, as she later told it: "Girl talk."

But Heezen was separately mapping earthquake epicenters, and the quakes kept landing along the same line as Tharp's rift. The coincidence was too exact. Within a few years the evidence snowballed into plate tectonics — the unifying theory of geology, as consequential as evolution for biology. The mid-ocean ridge turned out to be a single 40,000-mile mountain range, the largest feature on the planet, and the rift its open seam: the place where Earth continuously makes new crust. The planet has a wound that never closes, and it's where the world is born.

Tharp kept drawing. Her maps, painted into gorgeous physiographic panoramas with the artist Heinrich Berann, reached the public through National Geographic in 1977 and still define what most of us picture when we picture the seafloor. Her summary of the credit wars: "I was so busy making maps I let them argue." Later in life: "Not too many people can say this about their lives: The whole world was spread out before me."

And the twist: the ocean remains the great unknown. We have mapped essentially all of the Moon and Mars in high resolution; only about a quarter of the seafloor has been mapped with modern sonar. Satellites can't see through water; radar stops at the surface. Terra incognita never went away. It just sank.

Section 6: The extinction of lost.

Now consider the blue dot. A couple dozen satellites whisper timing signals; your phone triangulates; a serene circle announces: you are here. It is the most democratic cartographic achievement in history — billions of people carry a map better than anything a 16th-century emperor could buy.

And something quiet went extinct. Being lost used to be a common human experience — the wrong turn, the unfolding paper map across the steering wheel, the argument about whether to ask directions. London cabbies studying "the Knowledge" grow measurably larger posterior hippocampi; some studies suggest that leaning constantly on turn-by-turn directions lets that wayfinding machinery go slack. Park rangers coined the phrase "death by GPS" for people who follow the blue line into closed desert roads and beyond.

Urban planner Kevin Lynch argued we each carry a mental map built from five elements — paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks. That inner atlas is how a city becomes yours. The blue dot outsources it. And note: you can only be lost if you have some claim about where you ought to be. The dot abolishes the question, which is a strange kind of never being anywhere.

Closing: So, all maps lie. They must. But the lies differ in honesty. The best maps are the ones that confess — that show their seams the way Mercator's does if you know how to read it. And maybe that's the final thing maps teach: not where things are, but that the world is worth the trouble of describing — that it's knowable enough to attempt and strange enough to keep attempting. Every map, even a wrong one, is a wager that the territory rewards the trip.
